         COMES NOW the Office of the Public Counsel and for its Reply Brief states:

                                               Introduction

        Public Counsel’s reply is limited to its primary issues in this case where it believes

additional argument is warranted to inform the Commission during its deliberations. Those are

whether, or how, the Commission allows EMM to recover from Missourians through rates its

investment, costs, and expenses related to Mullin Creek #2 (Issues 20.B. and 32.D.); what return-

on-equity the Commission authorizes (Issue 1.C.); what EMM capital structure the Commission

authorizes (Issue 1.A.); and what of EMM’s investments in distribution and transmission projects

since its last rate case the Commission allows EMM to recover from Missourians through rates

(Issues 18.B., 19.A.&B., & 20.F.).

        As Public Counsel stated in its initial brief, nothing in any of the various stipulations and

agreements different parties filed in this case limits the Commission. Not only is the Commission

free to independently decide each issue limited only in that its decisions must be supported by the

record before the Commission, not arbitrary or capricious, and lawful, that is the role and

obligation for which the Legislature authorized it.

        The Commission has authority to authorize any person it employs to use the Commission’s

powers. 1 The Commission has the power to investigate and revise utility rates. 2 The Commission

has authorized persons it employs to act as a party in Commission proceedings such as this rate

case. 3 This means that when Staff is acting as a party in this rate case it is exercising Commission

powers that the Commission has authorized it to exercise.




1
  § 386.240, RSMo.
2
  § 393.140, RSMo., May Dep't Stores Co. v. Union Elec. Light & Power Co., 341 Mo. 299, 107 S.W.2d 41 (1937).
3
  20 CSR 4240-2.010(5) & (10).

                                                      3
            In its initial brief Staff cites to State ex rel. Monsanto Co. v. Pub. Serv. Com., 716 S.W.2d

791 (Mo. 1986), to support its assertion that “[t]he Commission may resolve all or part of a

contested case on the basis of a stipulation and agreement.” 4 What that case holds is that parties

were not precluded from continuing to challenge a rate design method the Commission adopted in

a rate case because they did not object to that same rate design method when the Commission

adopted it in the next subsequent rate case. In any event, the following quote from Judge

Blackmar’s dissent is not only applicable to opposed agreements, it also accurately characterizes

how the Commission should view all settlement agreements, and his analogy to a court soliciting

proposed findings and conclusions is apt:

           The procedural arguments in opposition to the Commission's order are not
           substantial. Complaint is made that the Commission adopted a nonunanimous
           stipulation, citing State ex rel. Fischer v. Public Service Commission, 645 S.W.2d
           39 (Mo. App. 1982), cert. denied 464 U.S. 819, 78 L. Ed. 2d 91, 104 S. Ct. 81
           (1983). The point is not well taken. The Commission was careful to avoid the
           problems in Fischer, in which there was a non-unanimous stipulation and a limited
           hearing. The Commission accepted the stipulation as representing the positions of
           the parties agreeing to it, and afforded the industrial users a full hearing with
           opportunity to offer all the evidence they desired on the points they placed in issue.
           Having done this, it was perfectly entitled to express its agreement with the
           stipulating parties and to make use of the stipulation in framing its findings and
           conclusions. The practice is similar to that of a circuit judge, who may invite all
           parties to submit requested findings and conclusions, and may then adopt and enter
           those which he considers to be supported by the record. 5

           Similarly to its initial brief, here Public Counsel has briefed further arguments on selected

issues, but by limiting its reply argument Public Counsel is not abandoning any arguments it raised

in its evidence or initial brief, and Public Counsel may not have cited to all of the evidence in the

record that supports its further arguments. Unless expressly waived in this brief, Public Counsel

 is not conceding any argument it has raised nor is Public Counsel abandoning any evidentiary

                                                      Argument

       1. Cost of Capital
       A. What is the appropriate capital structure to use for ratemaking in this proceeding?
           Public Counsel’s Position: The 45% common equity and 55% long-term debt
       ratemaking capital structure which Public Counsel witness David Murray determined is
       consistent with Evergy, Inc.’s more cost efficient targeted and average quarterly capital
       structure ratios for the period June 30, 2024, through June 30, 2026. Evergy Metro, Inc. is
       a subsidiary in a holding company structure where Evergy, Inc. is the ultimate parent.
       Evergy, Inc. issues equity and long-term debt in the capital markets through arms-length
       transactions with third parties. While Evergy Metro, Inc. does issue its own debt, its capital
       structure is managed through internal capital flows to achieve a common equity ratio of 52%
       at a specific point-in-time for ratemaking, which is the true-up date of June 30, 2026. By
       manipulating Evergy Metro Inc.’s common equity ratio to a suboptimal 52% common
       equity ratio Evergy is requesting the Commission to have Evergy Metro Inc.’s Missouri
       customers pay for a higher-cost capital structure than the capital structure which it targets
       for itself, despite the fact that legislative and regulatory changes in Missouri have shifted
       business risk from investors to ratepayers. Evergy Metro, Inc.’s Missouri ratepayers
       deserve credit for this shift in risk by being charged a rate-of-return that is consistent with
       Evergy, Inc.’s market-based capital structure ratios, ratios which Evergy, Inc. has
       dynamically managed to take advantage of its reduced business risk that flows to it from its
       regulated utility subsidiaries. 6


Public Counsel’s Reply Argument: In its initial brief, at pages 24-27, Staff asserts that it

examined EMM’s financing relationships with Evergy, Inc. before choosing to recommend the

Commission use EMM’s stand-alone capital structure for purposes of EMM’s Commission

allowed rate-of-return. Staff witness Dr. Won testified, “Evergy has not employed double leverage

in its financing history, based on the credit quality of EMM’s regulated utility business.” 7 He cites

to Staff’s Data Request No. 0123 as support for his testimony. While EMM’s response to that data

request is not in the record, it follows:




6
    See Ex. 205, Public Counsel witness David Murray direct testimony, Sch. DM-8, p. 2.
7
    Ex. 165, Staff witness Dr. Seoung Joun Won, Ph.D., surrebuttal / true-up direct testimony, p. 62.

                                                            5
            Question:0123

            Please explain whether Evergy Inc. has employed double leverage in its financing
           history, based on the credit quality of Evergy Missouri Metro’s regulated utility
           business. Requested by: Seoung Joun Won (seoungjoun.won@psc.mo.gov)

           Response:
           Evergy, Inc. has not employed double leverage in its financing history, based on
           the credit quality of Evergy Missouri Metro’s regulated utility business. Evergy
           Missouri Metro has an independently determined capital structure and issues its
           own long-term debt that is secured by its own assets, and not the assets of the parent
           company, to finance its rate base. Additionally, Evergy Missouri Metro and its
           issued debt securities have separate and distinct credit ratings from those assigned
           to Evergy Inc. by S&P and Moody’s.

Public Counsel’s point is that Staff relied on what EMM told it without undertaking any

independent analysis. Dr. Won did the same for his following direct testimony:

           Evergy has raised significant equity capital in recent years to support higher capital
           expenditures, including any necessary equity contribution into the utility, but no
           proceeds from Evergy long-term debt issuances have been used to infuse equity
           into EMM. Therefore, Staff does not find evidence that Evergy has used “double
           leverage” for investing in EMM. 8

There he relied on EMM’s response to Staff data request 347, which Public Counsel witness David

Murray attached to his surrebuttal and true-up direct testimony (Ex. ) as Schedule DM-S-3. That

response follows:

            Question:0347

           Please provide the list of financial records including amounts and dates that Evergy
           Inc.’s long-term debt issuances have been used to infuse equity into Evergy Metro
           Missouri since 2023 in an Executable MS Excel file. Requested by: Seoung Joun
           Won (seoungjoun.won@psc.mo.gov)

           Response:
           None




8
    Ex. 120, Staff witness Dr. Seoung Joun Won, Ph.D., direct testimony, p. 43.

                                                           6
            Instead of reporting the results of an independent Staff analysis Dr. Won merely relates

EMM’s self-interested responses to his data requests. The Commission should give no weight to

Dr. Won’s testimony and Staff’s argument based on it. Further, the Commission should discount

EMM witness Mr. Ley’s rebuttal testimony where he cites to Dr. Won’s finding that no double

leverage exists to attempt to corroborate EMM’s position to use the subsidiary capital structure. 9

Mr. Ley simply corroborated EMM’s response to Staff’s data request, not an independent finding

of Dr. Won. 10

           As Public Counsel related in its initial brief at pages five-to-eleven, Public Counsel witness

Mr. Murray analyzed in detail the capital flows between Evergy, Inc. and EMM since 2022. By

that analysis he discovered that before the creation of Evergy, Inc. in conjunction with the merger

of Great Plains Energy and Westar, EMM and its affiliates were distributing sufficient dividends

to pay third-party shareholders, but afterward they were not. Instead, Evergy began issuing debt

capital at the holding company level to fund dividends to third-party shareholders. Not only did

Mr. Murray discover this through his analysis of Evergy’s and its subsidiaries’ financial statements,

but EMM’s witness Mr. Ley stated to the Kansas Corporation Commission on November 20, 2024,

that this was Evergy’s strategy. Evergy’s credit quality arises from its ownership of low-risk

regulated utilities, including EMM. Evergy could not issue debt at the holding company and at

the subsidiaries (i.e. double leverage) but for its ownership of its vertically-integrated regulated

utility companies. In essence, because all of Evergy’s subsidiaries are low-risk regulated utility

companies, its business risk profile is the same as its subsidiaries.

           Staff’s assertion is that because Evergy, Inc. only owns regulated utilities using EMM’s

capital structure is appropriate; however, the opposite is true. Because Evergy, Inc.’s assets are


9
    Ex. 51, EMM witness Geoffrey Ley rebuttal testimony, p. 5.
10
     Ex. 207, David Murray surrebuttal and true-up direct testimony, pp. 12-13, & Sch. DM-S-3.

                                                          7
 essentially all wholly-owned, vertically-integrated rate regulated utilities, the most transparent

insight as to Evergy’s optimal capital structure to achieve the lowest reasonable cost of capital is

Evergy’s on a consolidated basis. EMM’s target of a 52% common equity ratio for ratemaking, if

adopted by the Commission, plays right into Evergy’s ability to maximize shareholder wealth by

creating higher cash flows achieved by charging EMM’s retail customers for a higher rate-of-

return; higher cash flows which create more funds to improve Evergy’s credit quality to allow it

to issue more holding company debt.

       On page 69 of its initial brief EMM asserts that EMM’s credit rating is distinct and superior

to that of Evergy, Inc. Given that Evergy, Inc.’s assets are essentially all wholly-owned, vertically-

integrated rate regulated utilities, the obvious question is “Why”? Why would not Evergy, Inc.

target EMM’s capital structure rather than the equity poorer capital structure it actually targets?

Public Counsel thoroughly explained in its initial brief how Mr. Murray explained why in his

testimony. In short, both explain that Evergy optimizes (targets a lower cost of capital) at the

overall consolidated group level, rather than at the level of each particular subsidiary. Doing so

allows Evergy to create an equity rich (higher cost of capital) capital structure for purposes of

ratemaking while still optimizing its capital structure at the consolidated group level. In short,

Evergy is attempting to charge EMM customers a higher cost of capital than it considers efficient

for itself. Despite EMM’s argument that its credit ratings are “distinct,” EMM’s credit ratings are

constrained by Evergy’s financial risk profile.

   C. What return on common equity should be used for determining rate of return?
      Public Counsel’s Position: 9.25%, the midpoint of Mr. Murray’s recommended
   authorized ROE range of 9.00% to 9.50%, a range which is based on the following
   considerations:
      • The electric utility industry’s cost of equity (“COE”) in 2015 was very similar to the
        current COE when this Commission authorized a 9.50% ROE for Evergy Missouri
        Metro;

                                                  8
        • Mr. Murray’s recommended 9.25% ROE fairly balances Every Missouri Metro’s
         shareholder compensation with the ratepayer burdens that Every Missouri Metro’s
         planned significant capital investments will create;
       • Every Missouri Metro will create additional shareholder wealth if it earns a ROE above
         its approximately 8.00% COE; and
       • 9.25% is reasonable under the Commission’s zone of reasonableness standard of 100
         basis points above and below recently authorized ROEs—here 9.70%, for a zone of
         reasonableness of 8.70% to 10.70%. 11


Public Counsel’s Reply Argument: In its initial brief EMM leads off its cost of equity

argument with, “The significant economic and geopolitical events that have occurred since this

case was filed on February 6, 2026, reinforce that it is appropriate for the Commission to

approve a return on equity in the range of 10.25% to 11.25%, as proposed by the Company’s

cost of capital witness Ann Bulkley.” 12 EMM asks the Commission to take notice that Treasury

yields have climbed since the end of the June 30, 2026, true-up cutoff date. 13 It charges, “Yet,

despite these dynamic times, in which a powerful American economy continues to be vexed

with rising inflation and interest rates, the ROE recommendations of Dr. Won for Staff and Mr.

Murray for OPC have remained static since they filed direct testimony based on data as of

December 2025.” 14 EMM is wrong. Public Counsel prefiled Mr. Murray’s direct testimony on

June 30, 2026, based on the most recent financial information available to him—information

through May 30, 2026. See e.g. Schedules DM-D-8 and DM-D-9 (Quarterly Capital Structures

June 30, 2024, to March 31, 2026) and bond and treasury yields graph January 2010 to May

2026 on p. 15. As Public Counsel stated in its initial brief (p. 18), in Mr. Murray’s over twenty-

five years of experience parties have always agreed (both formally and informally) that the only

 components of ROR that are subject to true-up are capital structure and the embedded cost of

long-term debt. The Commission should ignore EMM’s unfounded criticism.


     18. Plant in Service Accounting
     B. What amount of PISA deferral should be reflected in rate base?
         Public Counsel’s Position: To the extent that the $21.8 million for EMM’s lateral rebuild
     project, the $20.8 million for EMM’s substation projects, and $73.1 million for EMM’s
     transmission projects are included in the PISA deferral, the PISA deferral should be reduced
     to remove them before the PISA deferral balance is reflected in rate base.

Public Counsel’s Reply Argument: Because Public Counsel’s argument and witnesses for this

issue 18.B., and for issues 19.A., 19.B.; and 20.F. are so intertwined, rather than repeating them

they are all presented here under issue 18.B. EMM argues that the projects at issue qualify for

§ 393.1400, RSMo., plant-in-service accounting treatment.                 To qualify for that accounting

treatment the plant must be “qualifying electric plant” as defined by statute. That definition

follows:

        "Qualifying electric plant", all rate-base additions, except rate-base additions for
        new coal-fired generating units, new nuclear generating units, or rate-base additions
        that increase revenues by allowing service to new customer premises;

As Public Counsel pointed out in its initial brief, EMM imprudently failed to use a risk-informed

benefit-cost analysis for deciding whether to embark on its lateral rebuild, substation and

transmission projects. Recognizing the need for a benefit-cost analysis, EMM leans on Burns &

McDonnell’s proprietary AssetLens product offered by its 1898 & Co. division to satisfy that need.

After Public Counsel’s witnesses Dave Shapley testified that, with Paul Alvarez, he relied on The

Department of Energy’s Interruption Cost Estimate Tool for analyzing benefits and costs,15

EMM’s witness Jason D. De Stigter included a schedule to his rebuttal testimony which indicated

Shapley surrebuttal testimony, pp. 14-17.

                                                      10
 that Burns & McDonnell’s AssetLens product incorporated the DOE’s Interruption Cost Estimate

Tool. 16

           Staff was unable to assess how the AssetLens product EMM used works. 17 Based on his

prior experience Public Counsel witness Paul Alvarez questioned whether the AssetLens product

EMM used incorporated the DOE’s Interruption Cost Estimate Tool. 18 Further, Public Counsel

witness Paul Alvarez, who has some knowledge of it from multiple cases where utilities used it, is

under the impression that it is subjective in nature, and not a viable benefit-cost analysis tool.19

Public Counsel has raised a serious doubt of the prudency of EMM’s lateral rebuild project, and

certain of its substation and transmission projects putting the burden on EMM to show their

prudency, which EMM has failed to do. 20 For all the reasons Public Counsel argued in its initial

brief EMM has not established that these projects benefited its customers such that they should be

responsible for paying for them.


     19. Distribution Investment
     A. What level of distribution capital investment should be reflected in rate base?
         Public Counsel’s Position: For the reasons to which Public Counsel witnesses Paul
     Alvarez and Dave Shapley testify, the following amounts should not be included in rate base:
     $21.8 million for EMM’s lateral rebuild project and $20.8 million for EMM’s substation
     projects, a total of $42.6 million.

Public Counsel’s Reply Argument: See Public Counsel’s argument under issue 18.B., where

Public Counsel also presents its argument for this issue 19.A., as well as issues 19.B., and 20.F.

     20. Rate Base Components
     B. What amount of construction work in progress is appropriate to reflect in rate base?
         Public Counsel’s Position: None. The Commission has not determined in a §393.170,
     RSMo., proceeding the amount of construction work-in-progress that may be included in rate
     base. Further, as Public Counsel witness John Riley states, the combustion turbine
     prepayments that EMM is seeking to include as construction work-in-progress are pre-
     construction payments, not payments made for construction work-in-progress. 21 Additionally,
     unless the Commission holds data centers to their pledge and follows cost causation principles
     for to whom to allocate the costs of Mullin Creek #2, it should not include any construction
     work-in-progress in rate base. 22

Public Counsel’s Reply Argument: EMM appears to concede in its initial brief (pp. 99-100) that

the Commission must, as both Staff and Public Counsel argued in their initial briefs, determine in

a certificate of convenience and necessity case “the amount of construction work in progress that

may be included in rate base” before including it in rate base in a rate case. In other words, if the

Commission does not issue an order in Case No. EA-2026-0154 for the amount of construction

work in progress that may be included in EMM’s rate base for Mullin Creek No. 2 before it sets

rates in this case, then it would be error for the Commission to include any amount for construction

work in progress for Mullin Creek No. 2.

Counsel witness John A. Robinett direct, pp. 6-9).

      EMM also argues (pp. 100-101) that its turbine reservation fees qualify as construction work-

in-progress. Public Counsel still disagrees and has nothing to add to its argument in its initial brief

for its position that those turbine reservation fees are pre-construction costs, not construction work-

in-progress costs.

     F. What amount of transmission investment since EMM’s last rate case should be
        included in rate base?
        Public Counsel’s Position: For the reasons to which Public Counsel witnesses Paul
     Alvarez and Dave Shapley testify the following amounts should not be included in rate base:
     $73.1 million + $14.7 million = $87.8 million for EMM’s transmission projects.

Public Counsel’s Reply Argument: See Public Counsel’s reply argument under issue 18.B.,

where Public Counsel also presents its argument for this issue 20.F, as well as issues 19.A. and

19.B.


     32. Revenue Apportionment and Implementation
     D. How should revenue responsibility for construction work in progress be
        assigned or allocated among the customer classes?
        Public Counsel’s Position: It should be assigned entirely to the LLPS customer class.
     Public Counsel recommends that these costs be collected on the front-end to minimize investor
     and legacy ratepayer stranded asset risk.

Public Counsel’s Reply Argument: EMM and Google both argue that EMM is investing in

Mullin Creek No. 2 to serve all of EMM’s customers, not its LLPS customers. 23 It is not, EMM

is investing in Mullin Creek No. 2 to serve its LLPS customers.

        Mullin Creek No. 2 is a 440 MW gas unit.24 EMM is seeking to include $64,389,129 in

rate base as construction work-in-progress for Mullin Creek No. 2. 25 In its initial brief, EMM

argues, “Mullin Creek No. 2 is in any event a system resource designed to meet organic load

type appeared in the Company’s integrated resource plan as early as 2024,” citing to its witness

         As Public Counsel argued in its initial brief, to the extent that the Commission includes

construction work-in-progress investment in Mullin Creek No. 2 in EMM’s rate base, because the

cost causers of Mullin Creek No. 2 are future LLPS customer load and both state and federal policy

are that such cost causers should bear those costs they cause 33 the Commission should assign the

revenue requirement impacts of that investment directly to EMM’s LLPS customer class. 34 Rather

than repeating its support for that state and federal policy Public Counsel refers the Commission

to its initial brief.

                                                   CONCLUSION


         Public Counsel requests that the Commission adopt Public Counsel’s positions on the

issues, and Staff’s where Public Counsel has not taken a position, for the reasons set forth in Public

Counsel’s initial brief, this brief, and in the evidence, and adjust Evergy Missouri Metro’s rates
